title: Elegy
full_review:
Actress Bette Davis opined that old age is "not for sissies." And Leo Tolstoy declared the process was "man's biggest surprise."

Both quotes are invoked by Ben Kingsley's character in "Elegy" (Goldwyn), a somber but generally absorbing and impressively acted adaptation of Philip Roth's short novel "The Dying Animal."

Kingsley is David Kapesh, an aging -- and age-obsessed -- professor and cultural critic whom we first observe discoursing on the roots of puritanical repression on Charlie Rose's talk show on PBS.

We soon learn he's a womanizer with a jaundiced view of marriage. His estranged doctor-son, Kenny (Peter Sarsgaard), has never forgiven him for abandoning the family years before.

Unable to reconcile the paradox of aging and carnality, Kapesh sets his sights on doe-eyed student Consuela Castillo (Penelope Cruz), admiring her "elegant austerity" from the moment he sets eyes on her in class, but he dutifully waits to ask her out until graduation. A calculated theater date leads to an invitation back to his apartment, and an inevitable affair.

Commitment-phobic in the extreme, Kapesh doesn't even realize he's genuinely falling in love. And though Consuela has had boyfriends her own age, her affection for Kapesh is the real McCoy.

But Kapesh coolly continues to see his longtime mistress, Carolyn (Patricia Clarkson), at least until she comes across an intimate item belonging to Consuela in Kapesh's apartment.

Providing dubious counsel during all this is his best friend, George (Dennis Hopper), a Pulitzer Prize-winning poet, who advises him to eschew emotional involvement with the girl.

Kapesh ignores the advice, but just when it looks as though Kapesh is ready to take the first step toward commitment with Consuela -- an appearance at a gathering of her family and friends -- he can't bring himself to show up, and the affair seems to end. But subsequent events take the story in a surprising direction.

 

Director Isabel Coixet sensitively captures the story's themes of love, aging and death, and the film is artfully photographed by Jean-Claude Larrieu with penetrating close-ups of its excellent cast.

Cruz and Kingsley are in top form, the former arguably besting even her impressive work in "Volver," the latter evidencing a return to classy form after some questionable roles.

Though talky and characterized by the somewhat artificial air of many literary adaptations, the emotions are achingly authentic, and the end is unexpectedly moving, with redemption and greater understanding of self coming into play. The poignant bonding that eventually transpires between Kapesh and his son is an added plus.

The film contains nonmarital situations and nongraphic sexual encounters, upper-female nudity, frank sexual talk, adultery, abortion reference, some rough language and brief profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
